title: Missing
mood: A name on a board, a phone that does not ring, a room never entered before, and a bow nobody straightens.

hero.alt: In a dark room, the blue glow of a phone screen falls on two small dolls, one pink-haired and one dark-haired, leaning against a photo frame on a desk beside two little star charms.

segs.t: Guinevere knelt by the white wall with two fingers on her star. Her tie still hung half knotted. Far off, the city’s sirens went on and on.
She got up. She drew back her fist and hit the wall where the door had been.
The paint did not even crack. She hit it again, left and right, until her glove split across the knuckles and the white was smeared red.
Boots came down the corridor at a run.
Lesley came first, her long rifle on her back, a squad behind her. Her eye went over the broken Enders, the glass, the two black scuffs on the floor. Then it came to Guinevere.
Guinevere drew her fist back again. A hand took her by the arm and turned her away from the wall.
“There’s no time to lament,” said Lesley.
“I’m not lamenting. I’m getting in.”
“Not through that.” Lesley took a notebook and a pen from her coat and held them out. “Write down everything you saw. Now, while you remember it.”
Guinevere stared at the pen. Then she took it.
She sat under the windows with the notebook on her knee. Her knuckles bled onto the page. She wrote anyway, in big round letters that ran downhill.
Nine. Ten. “Then be faster.” I went ahead. Three steps. Purple light behind me. A second shadow over mine.
Her pen stopped there.
It came for my back,
she thought.
I left it open, and she stepped into it.
She wrote that down too. Then the rest. The glove on her shoulder, and the claw closing on the hand that pushed. The dark over her face.
She had left two words out. At the bottom she wrote them, and drew a line under them.
Stay back.

Chang’e had come in behind the squad, small among them, with a scanner as long as her arm. Mr. Bunny floated at her shoulder. She ran the scanner up the white wall, from the floor to as high as she could reach.
“Almost nothing,” she said to Lesley. “A door that small, inside the dome, where Enders already stood. That almost never happens.” She tapped the wall. “It cost them something to open.”
Guinevere looked up from the page. “So it was aimed.”
Chang’e looked at her. Then at the red smears on the white.
“I don’t know what it was,” she said.
Lesley held out her hand. Guinevere tore the pages out and gave them to her. Lesley read every line. Then she folded them into her coat.
By evening Lesley was pinning a new sheet to the board outside the Combat office. She pressed its corner flat with her thumb and walked away without looking at anyone.
VEXANA: MISSING.
It was in the same square type as a roster. Above it the watch sheet still hung, with their two names in print.
A boy and a girl had stopped behind Guinevere.
“Missing,” said the boy, low. “That’s what they write first.”
“She’s dead,” said the girl beside him. “They just don’t print that until later.”
Then they saw who was standing in front of them, and went.
Guinevere laid two fingers on her collar. Lit.
That night.
“Tonight, the hall,” she had said that morning. So she went to the training hall.
She lit every lamp in it. Whenever the hall stayed lit late, Vexana phoned. That was how it worked.
She did not lift a fist. She sat on the bench by the door with the phone face up beside her.
Then I’ll call,
Vexana had said at her door. Twice.
The hour came. The phone stayed dark.
She picked it up and looked at it. It was on. She turned the ringer up as far as it would go and set it down again, face up.
She knew what Vexana would say, flat as ever.
Go to bed.
“I’m asleep,” Guinevere told the phone.
You’re in the training hall,
said the voice in her head.
This time she did not say
I’m going.
She stayed on the bench.
Across the grounds, Vexana’s window in the girls’ wing was dark too. Guinevere waited a full hour anyway, under all that light over the empty floor.
Then she put out the lamps and walked back.
At her own door she took out the phone. Her thumb found Vexana’s name out of habit. It was always at the top.
It rang in her ear.
It rang somewhere down the corridor, too. Faint, behind a door.
She followed it.
Vexana’s door was shut. Guinevere had never been past it. She turned the handle, and it opened.

In the dark, a small screen lit up on the desk with every ring. It showed the photo from the hall, the two of them hand in hand, their badges new. Vexana had made it her wallpaper the day they got them.
Each time the screen lit, its light fell on two small shapes beside the phone.
The call rang out. The screen went dark. Guinevere found the lamp.

The room was nearly bare. A tin of oil, a jar of screws, two tactics books stacked square. The bed was made so tight it looked ironed. On the floor by the desk stood the old toolbox Vexana carried everywhere. This morning she had run out without it.
On the desk the same photo stood in a thin black frame. Beside it were the two shapes.
Two felt dolls. A pink-haired one with two bows of red thread, and a black-haired one. Each had a tiny yellow star stitched at its collar.
Guinevere knew those stars. She had made the real ones.
She did not touch the dolls.
A card was propped under them, written in small square letters. She knew that hand. It had written
I cannot repay this
on a note, on top of a pile of shopping bags.
For Guinevere. Same place, next year.
Her own words, from the roof. No
if
anywhere.
Beside the frame stood a white box. She knew that too. It had come out of the girls’ house with eight cakes in it, and she had put it into Vexana’s arms at the gate.
Midnight snack. That’s an order.
She lifted the lid.
Ticket stubs, a whole strip’s worth. A paper fan painted with goldfish. A paper napkin folded into a small square, a red smear of jam still on it.
She had put every one of those stubs into Vexana’s hand without looking. She had never asked where they went.
She sent back a whole coat,
she thought.
Every bag, folded. And she kept the napkin.
A laugh came out of her.
And I told her she didn’t need me.
Then she was crying. She held the box against her and did not wipe her face. The goldfish on the fan blurred.
There was nothing else in the box. No pink-haired keychain. That had swung at Vexana’s belt this morning, when she ran.
So she took me with her.
Guinevere reached for the card. Her hand stopped above it.
That’s hers to give me,
she thought.
Next year.
She sat down on the edge of the tight bed with the box on her knees. The dolls stood side by side in the lamplight.
“Without her, even the midday sun would freeze,” Guinevere told them.
The lid went back on. She set the box beside the frame, where it had been, and left the phone beside the dolls. Then she put out the lamp and pulled the door shut behind her.
In her own room she lay awake with her door open a hand’s width, as always, and listened down the corridor. Vexana’s door stayed shut.
At first light she tied her bows at the mirror. Her split knuckles had gone stiff in the night, and the left bow came out crooked. She pulled it loose and tied it again. It came out crooked again.
They were her mother’s bows. For years no hands but hers had touched them, and then Vexana’s.
Out in the corridor, the window was empty. Nobody stood there in running things, turning a page.
She touched the bow once. Then she left it as it was, and went down to the run alone.
That night she trained until her drones flew low and dim. She did not stop. In the middle of a combination her legs gave out under her, and she landed hard on her back.
A lady’s refinement,
she thought.
Three seconds.
“One,” she said. “Two. Three.”
She stayed down past three, and waited.
Nobody said “Four.”
In the end she got up without it.
The end of the first week.
In the training hall that night, Guinevere buckled on her arm guards under the lamp.
At her belt hung the black-haired keychain from the park. A little Vexana with a big head and long black hair. It had hung there since the day she pressed the pink one into Vexana’s palm.
You always had my back,
she thought.
And I never once looked.
She unhooked it from her belt. She clipped it to her arm guard, where her fist would swing.
It clicked into place.
So you go in front now. Where I can see you.
She lifted her fist into the light. The little doll hung under it. At her collar the star was lit, and somewhere, so was the other one.
“I will become a star shining in broad daylight and guide her,” she told the empty hall.
Then she turned to the bag. With every punch the little black-haired Vexana swung out ahead of her fist.
